name: Insurance Cost Allocation
plain_summary: A developer does not buy insurance one project at a time; it buys a programme -- a liability tower, a builder's risk policy over whatever is under construction, an excess layer above the primary. One premium arrives, and it has to become a number on each project's job cost: correctly, reproducibly, and summing back to what was actually paid. This engine reads the artifacts that allocation emits -- the policy register and its tower, the project register and its bases, the allocation schedule, the carrier audits, the job-cost ledger, the reporting summary and the general-ledger positions -- and runs twenty-four deterministic controls over them. Is the tower gap-free and every term continuous, does every project's share re-derive from its declared basis to the cent and reach only the projects the policy covers, did the carrier audit true-up return to the projects that bore the deposit on the basis they bore it, and does the allocation reach job cost and tie the ledger. It re-derives every share by the same largest-remainder method that produced it, compares each one with exact equality, and never writes to a source artifact.
marketing_thesis: The failures here do not look wrong in a column of six-figure numbers, which is exactly why they survive to the job-cost tie-out. An allocation of one premium across N projects leaves a residual cent; dropped it foots a penny short, double-counted a penny long, and either way the break surfaces months later as a tie-out nobody can source. A covered project whose basis value never arrived drops out of the weighting and silently moves every other project's share while the total still ties -- every individual share is wrong and nothing footed loudly. And a carrier audit lands after the term, when the open projects are not the ones that paid the deposit; crediting whoever is open today takes money from the wrong job. Footing to the premium is necessary and not sufficient. The engine re-derives each share where the penny actually landed, ships a planted-defect file for every registered control, and states its benchmark as a command rather than a claim.
layers_intro: Seven control families run in registry order over each programme file. The first proves the others had something to read and that the review date is legible, because a control that passes on absent evidence reports assurance it never performed.

layers.label: Structural Precondition
layers.plain: Checks the programme file carries every artifact the controls below read, exactly once, and that the review date is legible.
layers.engineering: set_complete runs first and deliberately owns the missing-artifact finding. It FAILs a file missing any of the seven document types in model.DOC_TYPES, or carrying more than one of any, because a control that silently passes on an absent input is worse than no control -- it reports assurance it never performed. It also FAILs when as_of is not a readable date, since the prepaid amortisation is measured to it. Every downstream rule returns nothing when its artifact is absent, so this precondition is what stops absence reading as a held control.

layers.label: Policy Register & Tower
layers.plain: Checks the policy register is sound and that the tower holds together with no gap in limit or in time.
layers.engineering: Five controls. pol_required_fields proves every policy carries the fields the allocation reads and that its line and layer are in the known vocabulary. pol_no_duplicate rejects a repeated policy number, which double-counts one premium in the programme total. pol_term_runs_forwards rejects an inverted term that would make the prepaid amortisation produce negative remaining days. pol_no_coverage_gap proves successive terms of the same line leave no uninsured day between them, and pol_tower_has_no_gap proves each excess layer attaches no higher than the primary limit beneath it -- both are the most expensive kind of clerical error in insurance, invisible until a loss lands in the band nobody bought.

layers.label: Allocation
layers.plain: Checks every share re-derives from its declared basis to the cent, sums to the premium, and reaches only the projects the policy covers.
layers.engineering: Seven controls and the core of the engine. alloc_basis_declared and alloc_basis_data_complete prove the basis is a known choice and that every covered project carries a usable value for it -- a missing value drops the project out of the weighting and silently moves every other project's share while the total still ties. alloc_project_exists and alloc_only_covered_projects prove the premium reaches exactly the covered schedule, in both directions. alloc_sums_to_premium is the footing identity, zero tolerance. alloc_shares_recompute is the control the engine exists for: it re-derives each share by the same largest-remainder method that should have produced it and compares each one exactly, so the residual cent is checked where it landed, not merely counted. alloc_no_negative rejects a negative share that nets to the right total and leaves two wrong numbers behind it.

layers.label: Builder's Risk
layers.plain: Checks builder's risk covers the right things, for the right term, at a value that tracks the budget.
layers.engineering: Three controls. br_value_ties_budget is the one deliberately tolerant rule, and it reads its band from the policy rather than inventing one -- an insured value well adrift of the hard-cost budget is either a project insured for less than it costs or a premium paid on money nobody is spending, so it FLAGs for review. br_term_covers_construction proves the term brackets the construction to the day, since cover that starts after the first delivery or ends before the last is a gap on the one asset that cannot be replaced from working capital. br_completed_project_removed FAILs a finished project still on the schedule, which keeps it in the weighting and makes every other project pay less than it should.

layers.label: Carrier Audit True-Up
layers.plain: Checks the audit true-up went back to the projects that bore the deposit, on the basis they bore it.
layers.engineering: Four controls. aud_true_up_sums proves the reallocation foots to the audit amount exactly. aud_credits_deposit_bearers is the control worth having: it compares the projects an audit credits against the projects the audited policy actually allocated to, because a carrier issues the credit months after the term and the open projects are no longer the ones that paid -- crediting whoever is open today is wrong in both directions at once, a project that never bore the deposit receives money and a closed project that did is never made whole. aud_uses_deposit_basis proves the split used the historical deposit basis rather than today's exposure, and aud_basis_restated FLAGs an audit that records no final exposure, so next year's deposit is not estimated from the figure this audit just corrected.

layers.label: Job Cost & Ledger
layers.plain: Checks the allocation reaches job cost and that the prepaid and programme totals tie the general ledger.
layers.engineering: Three controls that carry the allocation off the working paper and onto the books. gl_allocation_ties_job_cost proves what was allocated per project equals what actually landed on its job-cost ledger, because between the schedule and the accounting is a posting and a posting is where an allocation stops being arithmetic and becomes a number somebody reports on. gl_prepaid_amortisation_ties re-derives the unearned premium straight-line across the days of each policy term to the review date rather than trusting the number carried forward. gl_total_ties_programme proves the ledger's total insurance cost equals the sum of the policies written.

layers.label: Reporting
layers.plain: Checks the per-unit metric in the board pack recomputes from allocated cost and unit count.
layers.engineering: One control. rpt_per_unit_recomputes re-derives the per-unit figure as allocated cost floor-divided by unit count and FLAGs any that does not match. It is the figure that ends up in a board pack and the one nobody recalculates, which is exactly why it is worth recalculating -- a review signal rather than a hard failure, because it is a derived presentation number rather than the allocation itself.

blocks.label: Seeded Programme Files
blocks.plain: fictional insurance programme files enter the control registry
blocks.engineering: generate_corpus writes one clean baseline plus 25 planted-defect files, at least one for every registered control, 26 files in total. Only the projects, the policies and the audits are stated; every share, every reallocation, what lands on job cost, the per-unit metric, the prepaid balance and the programme total are derived, so the relationships the engine tests are the same relationships that produced the data.

blocks.label: Structural Precondition
blocks.plain: is the programme file complete and the review date legible
blocks.engineering: One control. FAILs a file missing any of the seven artifact types or carrying a duplicate, and FAILs an unreadable as_of, so no downstream rule holds vacuously on absent evidence.

blocks.label: Policy Register & Tower
blocks.plain: is the register sound and does the tower hold with no gap
blocks.engineering: Five controls: required fields and a known line/layer, unique policy numbers, forward-running terms, seamless renewals, and an excess layer attaching no higher than the primary limit beneath it.

blocks.label: Allocation
blocks.plain: does every share re-derive from its basis, to the cent
blocks.engineering: Seven controls: basis declared and its data complete, projects known and only covered ones charged, footing to the premium, each share re-derived by largest remainder, and no negative share.

blocks.label: Builder's Risk
blocks.plain: is the right thing insured, for the right term, at the right value
blocks.engineering: Three controls: insured value tracks the budget within the policy's own band, the term brackets construction to the day, and a completed project is off the schedule.

blocks.label: Carrier Audit True-Up
blocks.plain: did the true-up return to the projects that bore the deposit
blocks.engineering: Four controls: the reallocation foots to the audit amount, credits only the deposit bearers, splits on the historical deposit basis, and restates the final exposure it settled on.

blocks.label: Job Cost & Ledger
blocks.plain: does the allocation reach job cost and tie the ledger
blocks.engineering: Three controls: allocated cost equals what landed on each project's job cost, prepaid re-derives straight-line to the review date, and the programme total ties the ledger.

blocks.label: Reporting
blocks.plain: does the per-unit board-pack metric recompute
blocks.engineering: One control: the per-unit figure re-derives as allocated cost floor-divided by unit count, FLAGged rather than failed because it is a derived presentation number.

blocks.label: Project & Policy Registers
blocks.plain: the register and bases every allocation rule resolves against
blocks.engineering: The project register carries each project's code, stage, unit count and every basis value -- hard cost, insured value, unit count. The policy register carries each policy's line, tower position, term, premium, covered schedule and declared basis. Allocation, builder's risk and audit are all evaluated against these two authorities.

blocks.label: Verdict and Findings
blocks.plain: every finding, with the reason it exists, ends at a person
blocks.engineering: Findings roll up per programme file: any FAIL is FAIL, FLAGs without FAILs are REVIEW, clean is PASS. The CLI exit code is the verdict, so a pipeline can gate on it. Reports carry no timestamps or absolute paths, which is what makes the committed report diffable.

problem_statement: A residential developer does not buy insurance one project at a time; it buys a programme -- a general liability tower, a builder's risk policy over whatever is under construction, an excess layer above the primary. One premium arrives, and it has to become a number on each project's job cost, correctly and summing back to what was actually paid. Three failures hide inside that, and none of them look wrong in a column of six-figure numbers. Any allocation of one amount across N projects leaves a residual cent: dropped it foots a penny short, assigned twice it foots a penny long, and both surface later as a job-cost tie-out nobody can source. A covered project whose basis value never arrived drops out of the weighting and quietly redistributes every other project's share, while the total still ties to the premium -- every individual share is wrong and nothing failed loudly. And a carrier audit true-up lands months after the term, by which time the projects open today are not the projects that bore the deposit; crediting whoever is open takes money from the wrong job and never makes a closed one whole. None of these are judgment calls. They are equalities -- a share against its re-derivation, an allocation against the premium, a credit against the deposit bearers -- which a deterministic control settles better than a spreadsheet inherited by whoever holds it this year.

scenarios.title: The seeded demo runs every control over every programme file
scenarios.narrative: The CLI generates 26 fictional programme files -- one clean baseline and one carrying each of the 25 planted defects -- then runs all 24 controls over each. The clean file returns PASS with no flags; every defect file returns REVIEW or FAIL and names the control it tripped along with the reason that control exists.

scenarios.title: A cent moved between two projects keeps the footing
scenarios.narrative: A test moves one cent from one project's share to another's on the same policy. The footing control alloc_sums_to_premium stays silent because the total is intact by construction, and alloc_shares_recompute is the only control that sees the misplaced penny -- proof that summing to the premium is necessary but not sufficient.

scenarios.title: The true-up returns to the projects that paid
scenarios.narrative: A test moves a credit between two deposit bearers: aud_uses_deposit_basis fires because the split no longer re-derives on the deposit basis, while aud_true_up_sums stays silent because the reallocation still foots to the audit amount -- the same two-control structure that catches a credit routed to a project that never bore the deposit.

control_characteristics.plain: A clean result means the implemented mechanical controls found nothing wrong in the allocation they were given: every share re-derives from its declared basis, the programme foots and ties, and each true-up returned to the projects that paid. It is not an opinion on whether the allocation basis is the right basis, whether a project is adequately insured for its risk, or whether the programme was well bought.

verdict_map.action: carry the mechanically clean allocation into the documented job-cost and reporting review

verdict_map.severity: One or more FLAG, no FAIL
verdict_map.action: a human resolves each flag; an insured value adrift of the budget, an audit with no restated basis, and a per-unit metric that does not recompute all land here
the allocation does not go to job cost until the failing control is cleared

guarantees: Read-only: programme files are parsed and never written back, so the engine cannot introduce the break it reports.
Integer cents throughout, compared with exact equality; there is no tolerance band on the allocation, and the single tolerant control reads its band from the policy rather than inventing one.
A value that should be integer cents but is not produces an AMOUNT_INVALID finding contained to the one row it was read on, rather than being coerced into the number the engine is meant to audit.
Deterministic and byte-stable: same inputs produce the same findings in the same order, with no timestamps or absolute paths in any output.
Absent evidence is never a passing control; a missing artifact fails completeness rather than letting the controls that read it pass unread.

gate_policy.demo_gate: FAIL on the bundled corpus, by design -- it carries a planted defect for every registered control
gate_policy.note: The engine has no write path and therefore no autonomy to gate. It produces findings; a person decides whether an allocation goes to job cost.

limits.statement: The engine never posts an allocation, moves a premium, or writes to a source artifact. It reports and stops.
It reads the seven artifacts the allocation process emits. It does not connect to a broker system, a carrier portal, a policy-admin platform or the general ledger.

It is about where the cost lands, not whether a certificate is on file: certificate currency, limits and endorsements gate a payment, and the accounts-payable engine owns that gate. Nothing here re-checks a certificate.
It proves a share re-derives from the declared basis and ties, not whether that basis -- hard cost, insured value, unit count -- is the right one to have chosen. That judgment is a reviewer's.

All shipped data is fictional and the policy year is set in a fictional future. The corpus demonstrates the controls; it is not a record of any real programme, carrier, project, policy number or premium.

A footer strip reads 24 controls, 10,364 tests, read-only, SFS-E17-INS.
media.caption: The Insurance Cost Allocation engine tile states the identity that has to hold: one master premium split across every covered project's job cost, the residual cent landing where the largest-remainder method puts it, the tower closing with no gap, and each audit true-up returning to the projects that actually paid the deposit.

meta.description: Insurance Cost Allocation (SFS-E17-INS) datasheet -- twenty-four deterministic, read-only controls over a residential developer's insurance programme: the policy register and its tower, every project's share re-derived from its declared basis to the cent by the same largest-remainder method that produced it, the carrier audit true-up returned to the projects that bore the deposit, and the allocation tied through job cost to the general ledger. 10,364 tests, seeded fictional data, a planted-defect file for every control.
